summary: Provides protocol identifier examples that can be used to produce valid protocolDirTable INDEX encodings defined by the RMON MIB and the RMON Protocol Identifier Reference. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This is a book of worked examples showing how to write the wrapper codes the earlier document explained.

questions: what is rmon protocol identifier macro
how are rmon protocol ids encoded
subtitle: A catalog of worked examples showing how RMON-2 agents label protocol stacks such as ether2.ip.tcp.telnet.

tldr.problem: The RMON-2 MIB identifies each protocol encapsulation with a hierarchical OCTET STRING, and implementers need many concrete examples of how to build those strings for real protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER macros for the TCP/IP, Novell IPX, XEROX, AppleTalk, Banyon Vines, DECNet, IBM SNA and NetBEUI/NetBIOS stacks, plus multi-stack protocols, each showing how its children are selected and encoded.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and non-normative: an RMON-2 agent can be conformant without it, and the working group stopped maintaining it for lack of contributions.

today: RFC 2896 is an Informational memo and the text does not say it is obsoleted. It states that the working group discontinued maintenance of the macro repository, and that the normative encoding rules live in RFC 2895.

sections.title: What the Macros Are For
sections.content:
The RMON-2 MIB (RFC 2021) uses hierarchically formatted OCTET STRINGs to identify individual protocol encapsulations in its protocolDirTable. The syntax of the protocol identifier descriptor is defined in the RMON Protocol Identifier Reference.

This memo supplies examples of those identifiers. Each one is written as a PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER macro that can be converted to a valid protocolDirTable INDEX value using the mapping rules of the Reference document.

The memo says it is not an authoritative reference on the protocols it describes. Readers are sent to the Official Internet Standards document (RFC 2600), the Assigned Numbers document (RFC 1700) and other sources for complete protocol information.
sections.eli5: Network monitors need a name tag for every kind of traffic they count. This memo shows sample name tags so everyone writes them the same way.

sections.title: How It Relates to the Other RMON Documents
sections.content:
The first RMON-2 Protocol Identifiers document (RFC 2074) was split in two. The standards-track Reference portion became RFC 2895, and this memo holds the non-normative portion. It is meant to replace Section 5 of RFC 2074.

The split lets the examples be updated often without republishing any MIB objects or INDEX encoding rules. The base layer and IANA-assigned identifier macros stay in the Reference document because the RMONMIB working group defines those values.

The memo does not limit which protocols may be counted. An actual protocolDirTable may contain encapsulations not listed here, and may omit some that are listed. It is not relevant to any MIB other than the RMON-2 protocolDirTable.
sections.eli5: The strict rulebook lives in one document and the long list of examples lives in another, so the examples can grow without touching the rules.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Protocol Identifier Macro
sections.content:
Macros for network layer protocols sit right after a base layer identifier. The base layer identifiers the macros refer to are ether2, llc, snap, vsnap, ianaAssigned and 802-1Q.

A macro has PARAMETERS and ATTRIBUTES clauses. At the network layer the parameters are countsFragments(0) and tracksSessions(1), and the attributes are hasChildren(0) and addressRecognitionCapable(1). An agent may implement a subset of either, which limits which tables (protocol distribution, host, matrix) the protocol can appear in.

Other clauses describe how the protocol is nested. CHILDREN says how a child is selected, ADDRESS-FORMAT describes addresses, DECODING gives worked INDEX values, and the final ::= list says which parent identifiers the protocol attaches to. The protocol-name should be used for the ProtocolDirDescr field.

The examples are not meant to be exhaustive, but any protocol that can encapsulate other protocols must be documented so its children can be encoded into protocolDirID strings. A leaf protocol can be identified by an implementation even if it is not listed, as long as its parent is documented.
sections.eli5: Each macro is a small form: what the protocol is called, whether other things ride inside it, and which wrapper it sits in. Fill in the form and you get its code.

sections.title: Examples from the TCP/IP Stack
sections.content:
The largest part of the memo is Section 3.1.1, the TCP/IP stack. It starts with arp and ip, then lists the children of IP such as icmp, igmp, ggp, ipip4, st, tcp and egp.

Children of ip are selected by the one-octet Protocol field and encoded as [ 0.0.0.a ]. For example, the fragment 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.1 defines ether2.ip.icmp. Children of tcp are selected by the 16-bit source or destination port and encoded as [ 0.0.a.b ] in network byte order, so 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.6.0.0.0.23 identifies ether2.ip.tcp.telnet.

IP can be encapsulated in itself, so ether2.ip.ipip4.udp is a different protocolDirID from ether2.ip.udp, and the agent assigns two different local protocol index values to them.
sections.eli5: A parcel can have a box inside a box inside a box. The code lists each box in order, like a street address that goes from country down to house number.

sections.title: Other Protocol Stacks
sections.content:
After the TCP/IP stack the memo gives macros for several other families, each under its own heading: the Novell IPX stack, the XEROX protocol stack, the AppleTalk stack, the Banyon Vines stack, the DECNet stack, the IBM SNA stack and the NetBEUI/NetBIOS family. A final section covers multi-stack protocols.

Some of these protocols may no longer be in use, as the memo itself notes. They are included so that an agent which meets such traffic can describe it the same way another agent would.
sections.eli5: Besides the main internet language, the book also shows labels for many older network languages, in case a monitor sees them.

sections.title: Security and Maintenance Status
sections.content:
The security section says the document contains textual descriptions of well-known networking protocols, not the definition of any networking behavior, so no security considerations are raised by its publication.

On maintenance, the RMONMIB working group decided to discontinue upkeep of this repository document because the RMON vendor community was not contributing. It was published as an aid to implementing the protocolDirTable.
sections.eli5: It is only a list of examples, so it cannot cause any danger. The group that kept the list stopped updating it because nobody sent new entries.

viz.caption: THE ARP MACRO AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: arp PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER
data.code:
arp PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER
    PARAMETERS { }
    ATTRIBUTES { }
    DESCRIPTION
       "An Address Resolution Protocol message (request or response).
       This protocol does not include Reverse ARP (RARP) packets, which
       are counted separately."
    REFERENCE
       "RFC 826 [RFC826] defines the Address Resolution Protocol."
    ::= {
     ether2 0x806,   -- [ 0.0.8.6 ]
     snap   0x806,
     802-1Q 0x806    -- [ 0.0.8.6 ]
    }
